learningObjective: Explain why dead code elimination (DCE) in a tensor IR must respect ops that have side effects, and how the IR encodes this.

canonicalClaims.claim: DCE may remove operations whose SSA results are dead only when the operations have no observable side effects; writes to externally-visible memrefs (function arguments, escaping buffers) count as side effects and prevent elimination.
conditions: The IR distinguishes pure vs. side-effecting ops (e.g., MLIR's MemoryEffects interface).
Escape analysis (or the argument reachability) is available for the memory involved.
nonImplications: Does not imply DCE cannot remove any memref write; writes to fully-local, non-escaping buffers can be removed.
Does not imply DCE removes duplication (that is CSE).

misconceptions.claim: DCE removes any op whose result is unused, regardless of side effects.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Side effects on external memory or IO are observable even when the op's result is unused.

misconceptions.claim: Memref stores are always considered dead unless there is an explicit `sync` op.
misconceptions.whyWrong: IRs classify stores as side effects on the store's memory; no explicit sync is required for the store itself to matter.

misconceptions.claim: Pass-by-memref semantics allow the callee to elide writes it doesn't itself read.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The caller relies on the callee's writes; eliding them changes program semantics.

misconceptions.claim: DCE and CSE are the same optimization.
misconceptions.whyWrong: DCE removes dead operations; CSE deduplicates equivalent computations.

implementationFacts: MLIR uses the MemoryEffects interface to declare whether an op reads/writes memory
Local, non-escaping buffers can be optimized away when analysis proves no external observer
DCE typically runs multiple times together with CSE, canonicalization, and simplifications
performanceScenarios: Excessive conservatism in DCE keeps dead code; unsound aggressive DCE breaks correctness — both are common bugs in early-stage pipelines.
